title: Pie Graphs, Bar Graphs, Line Graphs and Stem-and-Leaf Plots
seo_title: Grade 7 Statistical Graphs Worksheets with Answers (MATATAG Math 7)
standard_text: Use appropriate graphs to represent organized data: pie graph, bar graph, line graph, and stem-and-leaf plot; interpret statistical graphs.
meta_desc: Free Grade 7 statistical graphs worksheets for the DepEd MATATAG curriculum: pie graphs, bar graphs, line graphs, stem-and-leaf plots and choosing the right graph. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Pie: parts of a whole. Bar: compare. Line: change over time.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • A pie graph (circle graph) shows parts of a whole. Each part's angle is its percent × 360°.
  • A bar graph compares categories. A line graph shows change over time.
  • A stem-and-leaf plot keeps every value: the stem is the tens digit and each leaf is a ones digit. Read the key: 4 | 7 means 47.
  • Before interpreting, read the title, the labels and the scale.

Examples

Example

25% of a pie graph

0.25 × 360°

Answer: 90°

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Percent as amountMultiply the percent by the total.
Ignoring the keyCheck what one stem and leaf mean.
Line graph for categoriesUse a bar graph for categories.

faq.q: What does MATATAG Math 7 ask about graphs?
faq.a: Use appropriate graphs to represent organized data (pie graph, bar graph, line graph, and stem-and-leaf plot) and interpret statistical graphs.

faq.q: When should I use a pie graph?
faq.a: When showing parts of one whole.
It shows the shape of the data and keeps every value.

faq.q: Can a bar graph be misleading?
faq.a: Yes, if the scale does not start at 0.

items.q: What percent of the learners take the bus?
items.e: Read the label on the Bus sector: 25%.

items.q: Which way of getting to school is used by the most learners?
items.e: The biggest sector has the biggest percent: Walk is 35%, more than Car (30%).

items.q: What percent of the learners do not walk to school?
What percent of the learners take the bus or ride a bike?
items.e: Add the two sectors: 25% + 10% = 35%.

items.q: What percent of the learners chose spring?
items.e: The sectors add up to 100%. 45% + 25% + 20% = 90%. 100% − 90% = 10%. (270 comes from 360 − 90: percents add up to 100, not 360.)

items.q: What percent of the learners chose basketball?
items.e: 30% + 25% + 15% + 10% = 80%. The whole circle is 100%, so basketball is 100% − 80% = 20%.

items.q: Which two subjects together make exactly half of the circle graph?
items.e: Half is 50%. Math 20% + Science 30% = 50%. PE and Art = 40%, Science and PE = 55%, Math and PE = 45%.

items.q: Which subject was chosen by one-quarter of the learners?
items.e: One-quarter is 25%. The PE sector is 25%.

items.q: Which sector is 110 of the circle graph?
items.e: 110 = 10%. The Music sector is 10%.

items.q: How many percent more learners chose apples than grapes?
items.e: Subtract: 40% − 15% = 25%. (55% adds the two sectors.)

items.q: How many learners take the bus?
items.e: 25% = 14. 14 of 80 = 80 ÷ 4 = 20 learners. (25 is the percent, not the number of learners.)

items.q: How many learners ride a bike?
items.e: 10% of 80 = 80 ÷ 10 = 8 learners.

items.q: How many learners walk?
How many more learners walk than ride a bike?
items.e: Walk: 36. Bike: 8. 36 − 8 = 28 learners. (35 is the difference in percent, not in learners.)

items.q: How many learners chose granola bars?
items.e: 1% of 200 = 2. 35% = 35 × 2 = 70 learners. (35 would be right only for 100 learners.)

items.q: How many learners chose yogurt?
How many learners chose fruit or yogurt?
How many learners chose lacrosse?
items.e: 10% of 60 = 6 and 5% of 60 = 3. 15% = 6 + 3 = 9 learners. (4 comes from 60 ÷ 15.)

items.q: How many learners chose volleyball?
items.e: 25% = 14. 60 ÷ 4 = 15 learners.

items.q: How many learners chose soccer?
items.e: 40% = 0.4. 0.4 × 60 = 24 learners. (2.4 puts the decimal point in the wrong place.)

items.q: All the angles at the center of a circle graph add up to …
items.e: A circle graph is a whole circle, and a full turn is 360°. (100 is for percents.)

items.q: A sector is 25% of a circle graph. What is its angle?
items.e: 25% × 360° = 0.25 × 360° = 90°. A sector of 25% is NOT 25°: it is one-quarter of the circle, a right angle.

items.q: A sector is 50% of a circle graph. What is its angle?
A sector is 10% of a circle graph. What is its angle?
A sector is 20% of a circle graph. What is its angle?
A sector is 35% of a circle graph. What is its angle?
items.e: 35% × 360° = 0.35 × 360° = 126°. (12.6° puts the decimal point in the wrong place.)

items.q: A sector is 15% of a circle graph. What is its angle?
A sector is 12.5% of a circle graph. What is its angle?
items.e: 12.5% × 360° = 0.125 × 360° = 45°. Check: 12.5% is 18, and 360 ÷ 8 = 45.

items.q: A sector of a circle graph has an angle of 90°. What percent is it?
items.e: 90° ÷ 360° = 0.25 = 25%. (90% reads the degrees as a percent.)

items.q: A sector of a circle graph has an angle of 72°. What percent is it?
A sector of a circle graph has an angle of 108°. What percent is it?
A sector is 13 of a circle graph. What is its angle?
items.e: 360° ÷ 3 = 120°. (33 is about the percent, not the angle.)

items.q: 24 learners were asked. 8 chose art. What angle should the art sector be?
items.e: Each student is 360° ÷ 24 = 15°. 8 × 15° = 120°. (Or: 13 of 360° = 120°.)

items.q: 40 learners were asked. 14 have a dog. What angle should the dog sector be?
In a pie graph of a family's budget, school expenses is 10%. What is the angle of its sector?
In a pie graph of a family's budget, the sector for rent is 108°. What percent of the budget is it?
In a pie graph of a family's budget, transportation is 30%. What is the angle of its sector?
In a pie graph of a family's budget, the sector for rice is 216°. What percent of the budget is it?
In a pie graph of a family's budget, rice is 15%. What is the angle of its sector?
In a pie graph of a family's budget, school expenses is 20%. What is the angle of its sector?
The number of runs scored by a cricket team are shown. How many values are in the plot?
items.e: Count the leaves, not the stems: there are 12 values.

items.q: The number of runs scored by a cricket team are shown. How many values are greater than 50?
items.e: Count the values above 50: 8.

items.q: The number of runs scored by a cricket team are shown. What is the largest value?
items.e: The last leaf in the last row: 59. Use the key to join the stem and the leaf.

items.q: The number of runs scored by a cricket team are shown. How many values are greater than 50?
items.e: Count the values above 50: 7.

items.q: The heights of tomato plants, in cm are shown. How many values are greater than 20?
items.e: Count the values above 20: 11.

items.q: The number of minutes learners spent on homework are shown. How many values are in the plot?
items.e: Count the leaves, not the stems: there are 12 values.

items.q: The masses of puppies at a vet, in kg are shown. How many values are greater than 50?
items.e: Count the values above 50: 9.

items.q: The masses of puppies at a vet, in kg are shown. How many values are in the plot?
items.e: Count the leaves, not the stems: there are 17 values.

items.q: The ages of people in a dance class are shown. How many values are greater than 45?
items.e: Count the values above 45: 9.

items.q: The number of minutes learners spent on homework are shown. What is the largest value?
items.e: The last leaf in the last row: 45. Use the key to join the stem and the leaf.

items.q: These values are put in an ordered stem-and-leaf plot: 20, 35, 12, 13, 29, 31, 36, 23, 36, 14, 31. Which is the row for stem 2?
items.e: Each value 20–29 goes on stem 2, with its ones digit as a leaf, in order. Repeated values keep every leaf: 2 | 0 3 9.

items.q: These values are put in an ordered stem-and-leaf plot: 62, 44, 64, 43, 66, 65, 59, 58, 62. Which is the row for stem 5?
items.e: Each value 50–59 goes on stem 5, with its ones digit as a leaf, in order. Repeated values keep every leaf: 5 | 8 9.

items.q: These values are put in an ordered stem-and-leaf plot: 11, 33, 37, 26, 29, 28, 24, 20, 25, 12, 33. Which is the row for stem 2?
items.e: Each value 20–29 goes on stem 2, with its ones digit as a leaf, in order. Repeated values keep every leaf: 2 | 0 4 5 6 8 9.

items.q: These values are put in an ordered stem-and-leaf plot: 34, 46, 48, 48, 39, 44, 26, 43, 20, 46, 34. Which is the row for stem 2?
items.e: Each value 20–29 goes on stem 2, with its ones digit as a leaf, in order. Repeated values keep every leaf: 2 | 0 6.

items.q: These values are put in an ordered stem-and-leaf plot: 43, 41, 33, 24, 43, 13, 44, 29, 40, 16, 34. Which is the row for stem 2?
items.e: Each value 20–29 goes on stem 2, with its ones digit as a leaf, in order. Repeated values keep every leaf: 2 | 4 9.

items.q: These values are put in an ordered stem-and-leaf plot: 18, 24, 33, 15, 30, 13, 37, 25, 35. Which is the row for stem 2?
items.e: Each value 20–29 goes on stem 2, with its ones digit as a leaf, in order. Repeated values keep every leaf: 2 | 4 5.

items.q: These values are put in an ordered stem-and-leaf plot: 41, 17, 19, 49, 18, 30, 33, 12, 38, 43, 36, 44. Which is the row for stem 3?
items.e: Each value 30–39 goes on stem 3, with its ones digit as a leaf, in order. Repeated values keep every leaf: 3 | 0 3 6 8.

items.q: These values are put in an ordered stem-and-leaf plot: 55, 48, 67, 77, 74, 64, 53, 65, 54. Which is the row for stem 7?
items.e: Each value 70–79 goes on stem 7, with its ones digit as a leaf, in order. Repeated values keep every leaf: 7 | 4 7.

items.q: These values are put in an ordered stem-and-leaf plot: 23, 21, 20, 35, 23, 35, 21, 31, 36, 28, 39, 20, 39. Which is the row for stem 3?
items.e: Each value 30–39 goes on stem 3, with its ones digit as a leaf, in order. Repeated values keep every leaf: 3 | 1 5 5 6 9 9.

items.q: These values are put in an ordered stem-and-leaf plot: 59, 67, 44, 48, 47, 57, 48, 69, 44, 56, 44. Which is the row for stem 6?
items.e: Each value 60–69 goes on stem 6, with its ones digit as a leaf, in order. Repeated values keep every leaf: 6 | 7 9.

items.q: Which graph is best to show the heights of 30 learners, grouped 140 to 150 cm, 150 to 160 cm and so on?
items.e: Height is continuous data grouped in equal intervals. A histogram shows this, with bars that touch.

items.q: Which graph is best to compare the favorite sports of the boys and the girls in a class?
items.e: There are two groups to compare in each category. A double (multiple) bar graph puts the two bars side by side.

items.q: Which graph is best to show how many learners in each grade walk, bike or take the bus, and each grade’s total?
items.e: In a stacked-bar graph, each bar is one grade. The parts of the bar show walk, bike and bus, and the whole bar shows the total.

items.q: Which graph is best to show the times of 50 runners in a 5 km race?
items.e: Time is continuous data. Grouping the times in equal intervals (20 to 25 minutes, 25 to 30 minutes …) and drawing a histogram shows how the times are spread.

items.q: Kenneth made a circle graph of his puppy’s mass each month. Why is this a poor choice?
c: The masses are not parts of a whole
items.e: Adding the masses from 12 months gives no useful whole. A broken-line graph shows how the mass changes.

items.q: What is missing from this circle graph?
items.e: Every sector is labeled, and the percents add up to 100%. But there is no title, so a reader cannot tell what the graph is about or who was asked.

items.q: Which list shows what every graph should have?
c: A title, labels and a source
items.e: A title says what the graph shows, labels name the categories and scale, and the source says where the data came from.

items.q: Where should the source of the data go?
items.e: The source, such as “Survey of 7B learners, October 2,026”, usually goes under the graph. It tells readers where the data came from and how much to trust it.

items.q: A bar graph will show values from 120 to 890. Which scale is best?
items.e: The scale must start at 0 and go past the biggest value, 890. Steps of 100 give 10 easy grid lines. (Going up by 1 needs 900 lines, and starting at 100 makes bars look wrong.)

items.q: A bar graph shows visitors to 4 parks. The biggest value is 4,800,000. Which scale is best?
items.e: Start at 0 and go up to a round number above 4,800,000. Steps of 1,000,000 are easy to read. (5,000 is far too small, and starting at 4,000,000 is misleading.)

items.q: Maria wants to show what part of her day she spends on each activity. She drew a broken-line graph. Which graph is better, and why?
c: Line plot: there are few values
Circle graph: parts of one day
items.e: The activities are parts of one whole day (24 hours). A circle graph shows each part of the whole. A broken-line graph is for change over time.

items.q: School A has 600 learners and School B has 300. Which graph lets you compare the NUMBER of walkers at each school?
items.e: Two circle graphs show percents, not numbers, so a bigger sector can mean fewer learners. A double bar graph shows the numbers side by side.

items.q: You have a table of counts. What do you do first to make a circle graph?
items.e: First add the counts to find the total. Then find each part as a percent of the total, and each angle as percent × 360°.

items.q: To change a percent into a sector angle, you multiply the percent by …
items.e: 1% of 360° is 360° ÷ 100 = 3.6°. So 25% is 25 × 3.6° = 90°. (Multiplying by 1 gives the mistake 25% = 25°.)

items.q: A sector is 40% of a circle graph. What is its angle?
items.e: 40% × 360° = 0.4 × 360° = 144°. (14.4° puts the decimal point in the wrong place, and 160° multiplies by 4 instead of 3.6.)

items.q: Favorite lunch of 60 learners: pizza 21, sushi 15, tacos 12, soup 9, salad 3. What percent should the pizza sector show?
items.e: 2160 = 21 ÷ 60 = 0.35 = 35%. (39 learners did not choose pizza, and 42 doubles 21, which works only for a total of 50.)

items.q: Favorite lunch of 60 learners: pizza 21, sushi 15, tacos 12, soup 9, salad 3. How many degrees stand for each student?
items.e: 360° ÷ 60 = 6° for each student. (3.6° is 1%, not one student.)

items.q: Favorite lunch of 60 learners: pizza 21, sushi 15, tacos 12, soup 9, salad 3. What angle should the sushi sector be?
items.e: 15 × 6° = 90°. (25 is the percent, not the angle, and 150 uses 10° for each student.)

items.q: Favorite lunch of 60 learners: pizza 21, sushi 15, tacos 12, soup 9, salad 3. What angle should the salad sector be?
items.e: 3 × 6° = 18°. (5 is the percent, and 30 uses 10° for each student.)

items.q: A table shows that 5 of 24 learners chose soccer. What angle should the soccer sector be?
items.e: Each student is 360° ÷ 24 = 15°. 5 × 15° = 75°. (21 is about the percent, and 50 uses 10° for each student.)

items.q: What percent of the learners take the bus?
items.e: Read the label on the Bus sector: 35%. (65% is everyone else, and 126 is the angle of the sector in degrees.)

items.q: What is the angle of the Walk sector?
items.e: 30% × 360° = 0.3 × 360° = 108°. (30° reads the percent as degrees, 10.8° puts the decimal point in the wrong place, and 252° is the rest of the circle.)

items.q: The class has 40 learners. How many take the bus?
items.e: 35% of 40 = 0.35 × 40 = 14 learners. (35 is the percent, 26 learners do not take the bus, and 140 forgets to divide by 100.)

items.q: What percent of the learners chose spring?
items.e: 40% + 25% + 20% = 85%. The whole circle is 100%, so spring is 100% − 85% = 15%. (275 subtracts from 360: percents add up to 100, not 360.)

items.q: What percent of Ivan’s day is school?
items.e: 90° ÷ 360° = 0.25 = 25%. (90 is the angle, and 6 is the number of hours.)

items.q: How many hours does Ivan sleep?
items.e: The whole day, 24 hours, is 360°, so 1 hour is 360° ÷ 24 = 15°. 135° ÷ 15° = 9 hours. (13.5 divides by 10, and 37.5 is the percent.)

items.q: Which sector is 18 of Ivan’s day?
items.e: 18 of 360° = 45°. The Sports sector is 45° (3 hours). (Homework is 30° and Other is 60°.)

items.q: A sector of a circle graph has an angle of 54°. What percent is it?
items.e: 54° ÷ 360° = 0.15 = 15%. (54% reads the degrees as a percent.)

items.q: How many viewers watched by streaming?
items.e: 35% of 2,400,000 = 0.35 × 2,400,000 = 840,000 viewers. (84,000 and 8,400,000 have the place value wrong, and 1,560,000 is everyone else.)

items.q: How many more viewers watched on TV than on the radio?
items.e: TV − radio = 55% − 10% = 45%. 45% of 2,400,000 = 0.45 × 2,400,000 = 1,080,000 viewers. (45 is the difference in percent, 1,320,000 is the TV viewers only, and 108,000 has the place value wrong.)

items.q: To draw a fair bar graph of this data, where should the scale start?
items.e: Bar heights can be compared fairly only when the scale starts at 0. Then the bars are 58 and 52 high and look almost the same.

items.q: How many more cans were collected in 2,026 than in 2,022?
By what percent did the number of cans grow from 2,022 to 2,026?
items.e: Growth = 250 cans. 250 ÷ 2,500 = 0.1 = 10%. (250% reads the cans as a percent, 25% divides by 1,000 instead of 2,500, and 100% would mean doubling: the steep line makes it look that way because the scale starts at 2,500.)

items.q: A poster says, “Our food drive more than doubled!” Is this supported?
items.e: Doubling 2,500 gives 5,000. The school collected 2,750, only 10% more. The scale starts at 2,500, so the line looks steeper than it is.

items.q: Which school has more learners who walk?
items.e: School A: 20% of 600 = 120. School B: 40% of 300 = 120. The Walk sector is twice as big at School B, but School B has half as many learners.

items.q: How many more learners take the bus at School A than at School B?
items.e: School A: 45% of 600 = 270. School B: 30% of 300 = 90. 270 − 90 = 180 learners. (15 is the difference in percent.)

items.q: A circle graph shows that 25% of the 1,200 learners at a school chose volleyball. A reporter writes, “25 learners chose volleyball.” What is wrong?
items.e: A percent is a part of the total. 25% of 1,200 = 1,200 ÷ 4 = 300 learners. (48 comes from 1,200 ÷ 25.)

items.q: In a random survey of 400 learners in a school board, 35% said they walk to school. The board has 18,000 learners. About how many of them walk?
items.e: Use the sample percent for the whole board: 35% of 18,000 = 0.35 × 18,000 = 6,300 learners. (140 is 35% of the 400 in the sample, and 11,700 are the ones who do not walk.)

items.q: A city has 750,000 adults. In a random survey of 1,500 of them, 42% said they skate in winter. About how many adults in the city skate?
items.e: 42% of 750,000 = 0.42 × 750,000 = 315,000 people. (630 is 42% of the sample, 31,500 has the place value wrong, and 435,000 are the other 58%.)

items.q: A bar graph’s scale is labeled 0, 10, 20, 100, 500, with equal spaces between the labels. Why is it misleading?
items.e: The space from 0 to 10 is the same as the space from 100 to 500, but one is 10 and the other is 400. Bars on this scale cannot be compared fairly.
